title: Ghost Stories Of Crewkerne, Somerset
excerpt: Crewkerne is an ancient Somerset market town surrounded by old roads, lonely hills and some wonderfully strange ghost stories
content:
Crewkerne may be small, but it has been around for a very long time.

The Somerset market town has Saxon roots and was once important enough to have its own royal mint. Later, the cloth and sailcloth trades brought prosperity to the town.

Beyond its historic streets lie country lanes, former coaching routes and the high ground towards Windwhistle and Chard.

Here are five haunted places and legends to discover in and around Crewkerne.

Sandy Road, Crewkerne

One of Crewkerne’s oldest ghost stories concerns Sandy Road.

The tale was recorded by local historian George F. Munford, whose writings preserved many older stories from the area.

Known as The Ghost of Sandy Road, the account belongs to the long tradition of apparitions encountered by travellers after dark.

Unfortunately, the precise spot connected with Munford’s ghost is difficult to establish today.

Nevertheless, it remains one of the supernatural stories most directly associated with Crewkerne itself.

The Haunted House of Crewkerne

Somewhere in Crewkerne once stood a house with a decidedly spooky reputation.

Evidence for the haunting survives in the University of Leeds folklore sound archive, which preserves recordings of Somerset residents discussing local traditions.

One recording features Eddie Wills, Mrs Wills and their son talking about a haunted house in Crewkerne.

The story becomes stranger with claims of an underground passage connecting the house with an old friary.

Secret tunnels are common in British folklore, particularly around churches, monasteries and ancient houses.

Sadly, the archive catalogue does not provide a reliable modern address for the property.

The identity of Crewkerne’s mysterious haunted house therefore remains unknown.

The Old Parsonage

Another Crewkerne tradition concerns an old parsonage haunted by a strange female apparition.

Rather than the familiar White Lady, witnesses reportedly described something less distinct – a hazy human figure.

Old rectories and parsonages have produced countless English ghost stories, often involving former residents who apparently never left.

The difficulty here is identifying exactly which Crewkerne property lies behind the tradition.

Without stronger evidence, the story is best treated as part of the town’s traditional ghost lore rather than a confirmed haunting.

Ghosts of the Crewkerne to Chard Road

A30, between Crewkerne and Chard, Somerset

The old road west from Crewkerne towards Chard has several strange traditions attached to it.

One of the most colourful involves phantom smugglers apparently fighting beside the road.

Witnesses reportedly saw figures struggling before the scene disappeared, leaving the road empty once again.

Whether smugglers actually fought here is uncertain. Smuggling became deeply embedded in southern English folklore, with stories spreading well beyond the coast.

The setting certainly helps.

Outside Crewkerne, the road quickly becomes rural, passing wooded countryside and lonely stretches before climbing towards Windwhistle.

And that’s where things become even stranger.

Windwhistle and Cricket St Thomas

Windwhistle, Cricket St Thomas, near Crewkerne, Somerset

A few miles west of Crewkerne lies Windwhistle, home to some of the area’s best supernatural folklore.

Recordings preserved by the University of Leeds include stories about a ghostly coach around Windwhistle.

Phantom coaches once appeared regularly in British folklore. Travellers reported hearing invisible horses and wheels or seeing coaches that suddenly vanished.

Windwhistle also has traditions involving a spectral black dog and the sound of chains.

Black dogs are among the most sinister figures in English folklore. They traditionally appear on lonely roads, near churchyards and at places associated with death.

Some were considered omens, while others simply appeared before mysteriously disappearing.

The old Windwhistle Inn, now the Cricket St Thomas Country Inn, recalls the days when travellers crossed this high ground by horse and coach.

With ghost coaches, phantom dogs and lonely roads, Windwhistle is an appropriately spooky finish to our journey.

Haunted Crewkerne

Crewkerne doesn’t have the haunted fame of Glastonbury or Dunster, but perhaps that’s part of its appeal.

Its ghosts survive mainly through local histories, folklore and memories rather than organised ghost tours.

There’s the Ghost of Sandy Road, a mysterious haunted house, a hazy woman and phantom smugglers fighting beside an old road.

Then, just beyond town, Windwhistle adds ghost coaches and spectral black dogs to the mix.

For a quiet Somerset market town, Crewkerne has gathered a remarkably lively population of the dead.
